newsitem.title: USA: Ten years is too short a time for AIDS vaccine-expert.
newsitem.headline: Ten years is too short a time for AIDS vaccine-expert.

text.p: The head of the National Institutes of Health AIDS Vaccine Research Committee said on Thursday that 10 years was an "unreasonably short time" in which to produce an effective AIDS vaccine.
President Bill Clinton called on May 18 for a "new national goal for science" to develop a vaccine for AIDS within the next 10 years.

"If you mean by 'develop a vaccine' have a vaccine in the field working to protect people, then 10 years is an unreasonably short time, because it often takes 10 years from the time that you have a good candidate before you're convinced it actually works in the field," Dr. David Baltimore told reporters at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research.

"If you say what he meant by development of a vaccine is to have a good vaccine candidate -- then I'd say that's a reasonable timeline," said Baltimore, a Nobel prize winner who will become president of California Institute of Technology next fall.

Currently a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Baltimore compared current chemotherapy and multi-drug drug cocktail treatments for AIDS as being akin to the "iron-lung" stage of treatment for polio.
"In my committee we have taken the approach of supporting any vaccine strategy which seems in the slightest to be potentially beneficial ... we don't know what will work," he said.
